candidates.title: Review multi-agent answer drift

demandEvidence.chore: Review whether a multi-agent answer adds unsupported inferences or edge cases compared with its source request.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: How does this not end up in a chinese whisper game, especially considering how much LLMs infer, guess, and find edge cases and whatnot everywhere?

ease.reason: A supplied original question gives a clear drift concern, but no implementation reference is attached.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: professional teams coordinating multi-agent work may pay for review help; this question establishes no buying intent.

feasibility.reason: A small manual comparison prototype is bounded, but useful drift criteria and representative inputs are unverified.

autonomy.reason: A comparison can repeat on supplied transcripts; a person must define truth and inspect flagged differences.

evidence.reason: The literal question identifies concern about inferred additions in chained LLM work, but provides no frequency or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A comparison report that flags where a multi-agent final answer adds claims absent from the initial request or supplied notes.
inputs: Operator-written expected facts and allowed inferences
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator submits a completed multi-agent run for review.
steps: Split the initial request and supplied notes into operator-approved facts.
Compare each final-answer claim with those facts using a fixed checklist.
Mark claims as supported, absent, or ambiguous.
Produce a short report linking each flag to the supplied text.
Ask a reviewer to correct the report before using it.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a small hand-labeled set, check whether each deliberately inserted unsupported claim is flagged and supported claims are not mislabeled.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A reviewer supplies representative transcripts, defines what counts as an allowed inference, checks every flag, and decides whether to change the workflow.
unverified: No supplied source documents transcript comparison software or reliable claim attribution.
Accuracy on real multi-agent workflows and acceptable false-alarm rates are unknown.

candidates.reason: Assessed because the source gives a concrete stated concern or workflow; the scoped experiment remains below the six-point threshold and has no validated payer.

candidates.title: Track app-review follow-ups

demandEvidence.chore: Track a submitted app review and prepare a status inquiry when no update has arrived.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: What is your goal? Get our custom app Elfsight AI Chatbot reviewed and approved. What is the problem & what have you tried? The app was submitted for review on September 3, 2026. It has been in “Review process started” status for 55 days, and we haven’t had any updates. Could you please share an estimated timeline, or let us know if anything is needed from our side?

ease.reason: Operator-entered submission dates and status can support a basic follow-up draft; portal access is unsupported.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: app developers might pay for review tracking, but this single request proves no market or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week reminder and draft prototype is bounded; status accuracy and useful follow-up timing remain unknown.

autonomy.reason: A draft reminder can recur from entered dates, while a person must verify status and send it.

evidence.reason: The retained span specifies one pending review and asks about timing or missing items, without recurrence or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A dated queue of app-review follow-ups with a draft message based only on operator-entered status and dates.
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator adds or updates an app review record.
steps: Calculate elapsed days from the supplied dates.
Compare the record with an operator-chosen follow-up interval.
Draft a concise status inquiry from the supplied facts only.
Show the draft and source fields for review.
Record whether the operator sent, edited, or skipped it.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For fictional records, verify elapsed-day calculations and confirm each draft contains only supplied facts and leaves the send decision to the reviewer.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person enters and verifies status, chooses follow-up intervals, approves wording, and sends any message.
unverified: No source supports access to a review portal or status monitoring.
The useful interval and wider recurrence of this chore are unknown.

candidates.reason: Assessed because the source gives a concrete stated concern or workflow; the scoped experiment remains below the six-point threshold and has no validated payer.

candidates.title: Check weekly keyword metric rows

demandEvidence.chore: Prepare weekly keyword rows containing search volume, CPC and difficulty in a spreadsheet.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Runs VNCNT Labs’ Keyword Search Volume Actor on Apify every week and adds each keyword’s Google search volume, CPC and difficulty as rows in Google Sheets. Connect your own Apify and Google accounts after importing. The schedule is Monday 9 am UTC and can be changed. I maintain the Actor; it’s pay per result on Apify ($0.003 per Google keyword plus $0.05 per batch). The flow JSON is available on request.

ease.reason: The retained workflow gives specific weekly fields and a sheet output, but actor execution and account connections are unsupported here.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: independent marketing consultants may pay for recurring keyword reports; this showcase does not prove buyer demand.

feasibility.reason: A row-checking mock is bounded; accurate metrics, Apify access and Sheets writes remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A scheduled row format is described in the post, but the proposed student loop still needs a person to verify inputs and output.

evidence.reason: The post names weekly volume, CPC and difficulty rows and schedule, but is a single shared workflow rather than corroborated demand.

experimentPlan.output: A weekly table that checks supplied keyword metric rows for missing fields, duplicate keywords, and large week-to-week changes.
inputs: Synthetic volume, CPC and difficulty rows
Operator-chosen required columns and change flags
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator uploads a weekly metric table.
steps: Check that each row has the chosen keyword and metric columns.
Flag duplicate keywords and missing values.
Compare current and prior supplied values.
Mark changes for human review without inventing explanations.
Return a review table for operator correction.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: With fictional current and prior tables containing known blanks, duplicates, and changed values, verify every flag and ensure unchanged rows stay unflagged.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person obtains authorized metrics, supplies both tables, chooses useful thresholds, and verifies changes before acting.
unverified: The post describes an existing Actor and Sheets flow, but no supplied implementation reference establishes those capabilities for this proposal.
Live metric retrieval, API cost, and customer demand are unverified.

candidates.reason: Assessed because the source gives a concrete stated concern or workflow; the scoped experiment remains below the six-point threshold and has no validated payer.

candidates.title: Draft shipment delay notices

demandEvidence.chore: Notify a dispatcher when a shipment is delayed.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: A simple flow can notify a dispatcher when a shipment is delayed, copy an order update into a CRM, alert a buyer when inventory drops, or send a daily report to a team channel.

ease.reason: Synthetic shipment rows make a draft alert mock approachable; no supplied reference supports live logistics intake.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: logistics operators may pay for clearer exception notices; these examples establish no buying intent.

feasibility.reason: A four-week sample-row draft test is bounded; real event access and correct delay rules remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A repeatable draft can follow supplied rows, but a person must verify status and approve any notice.

evidence.reason: The retained task span lists concrete notification examples, but gives no specific case, recurrence or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A review table that turns operator-supplied shipment-delay rows into draft dispatcher notices.
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator uploads or enters a shipment status row.
steps: Check required fields and compare dates with the operator-set threshold.
Flag rows that meet the proposed delay rule.
Draft a notice using only supplied status and order fields.
Show the row, reason for flag, and draft together.
Have a dispatcher verify status and approve or discard the notice.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On fictional rows with known dates and threshold, check which rows are flagged and whether each draft matches its row without adding facts.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A dispatcher supplies and verifies records, sets the threshold, and approves every notice; live carrier and CRM access are excluded.
unverified: The article gives examples but no logistics field schema or repeated customer evidence.
No supplied reference supports live event intake or message delivery.

candidates.reason: Assessed because the source gives a concrete stated concern or workflow; the scoped experiment remains below the six-point threshold and has no validated payer.

candidates.title: Review site pages for usefulness

demandEvidence.chore: Review site pages for whether they answer a question or solve a problem, and remove pages that do not.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Before adding anything new I check whether the page already has a reason to exist. If it does not answer a question or solve something, I delete it.

ease.reason: A person can test a checklist on supplied page text, but no page-crawling or content-analysis capability is documented.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small site owners might pay for page audits; this one personal tip gives no buyer or payment evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week report prototype can review operator-supplied page text; useful criteria and evaluation against real sites remain uncertain.

autonomy.reason: A repeatable checklist can flag pages from supplied text, while a person must judge value and approve every removal.

evidence.reason: The native span explicitly describes checking whether a page answers a question or solves a problem and deleting it, but gives no frequency or corroboration.

experimentPlan.output: A review table listing supplied site pages, the question or problem each appears to address, and pages needing human review.
inputs: Operator-supplied page URLs and visible text
Synthetic examples with clear and unclear page purpose
experimentPlan.trigger: A site owner supplies a batch of pages for a periodic content review.
steps: Read each supplied page title and text without changing the live site.
Compare its stated purpose with the operator-provided audience and site purpose.
Draft a short reason when the supplied text appears not to answer a question or solve a problem.
Mark ambiguous pages for manual review instead of recommending removal.
Return a table with page, proposed purpose, concern, and reviewer decision.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Using fictional pages labeled by a site owner, check that the report flags only pages the supplied text does not connect to the stated audience need and leaves ambiguous cases for review.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies permitted page text, defines the audience and usefulness criteria, checks every finding, and authorizes any deletion; the proposed tool never changes a live site.
unverified: No supplied implementation reference supports crawling, parsing, or monitoring live websites.
The source provides one personal tip, so repeated workload and wider customer demand are unknown.
Whether page usefulness can be judged reliably from text alone is unresolved.

candidates.reason: Concrete chore assessed as requested by repair feedback; the scoped report is plausible to prototype, but the documented single personal example and unsupported live-site capabilities leave the provisional mean below six.
